claims.text: An AWD-LSTM language model is trained on WikiText-103 to learn general language representations.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'we pretrain the language model on Wikitext-103 (Merity et al., 2017b)' and 'we use the state-of-the-art language model AWD-LSTM (Merity et al., 2017a)'.

claims.text: ULMFiT consists of three primary stages: general-domain LM pretraining, target task LM fine-tuning, and target task classifier fine-tuning.
claims.reason: Paper explicitly lists three steps in Section 3: '(a) General-domain LM pretraining, (b) target task LM fine-tuning, and (c) target task classifier fine-tuning'.

claims.text: Discriminative fine-tuning applies different learning rates to different layers, as different layers capture different types of information.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'discriminative fine-tuning allows us to tune each layer with different learning rates' and 'different layers capture different types of information'.

claims.text: STLR is a learning rate schedule that linearly increases and then linearly decays.
claims.reason: Paper defines STLR as one that 'first linearly increases the learning rate and then linearly decays it'.

claims.text: Gradual unfreezing starts from the last layer and progressively unfreezes lower layers to prevent catastrophic forgetting.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'we propose to gradually unfreeze the model starting from the last layer... We first unfreeze the last layer and fine-tune all unfrozen layers for one epoch. We then unfreeze the next lower frozen layer'.

claims.text: The study evaluates the model on six widely-studied text classification benchmarks.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'We evaluate our method on six widely-studied datasets' and Table 1 lists six datasets.

claims.text: Benchmarks include IMDb, Yelp-bi, Yelp-full (sentiment analysis), TREC-6 (question classification), AG News and DBpedia (topic classification).
claims.reason: Table 1 in the paper lists all six datasets: TREC-6, IMDb, Yelp-bi, Yelp-full, AG, and DBpedia, with their respective task types.

claims.text: TREC-6 is the six-class version of the TREC dataset.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'We use the six-class version of the small TREC dataset' and Table 1 shows TREC-6 has 6 classes.

claims.text: Model performance is assessed using test error rates (%), where a lower value indicates better performance.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'For consistency, we report all results as error rates (lower is better)'.

claims.text: ULMFiT is compared against CoVe and CNN baselines.
claims.reason: Paper compares against 'CoVe (McCann et al., 2017), a state-of-the-art transfer learning method' and CNN-based models like 'Char-level CNN (Zhang et al., 2015)' and 'DPCNN (Johnson and Zhang, 2017)'.

claims.text: The paper tests 'low-shot' scenarios measuring performance when only 100 labeled examples are available.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'at 100 labeled examples, we match the performance of training from scratch with 50x and 100x more data' and Figure 3 shows experiments with 100 labeled examples.

claims.text: ULMFiT achieves competitive performance with 100x fewer labeled examples than training from scratch.
claims.reason: Paper states: 'with only 100 labeled examples, it matches the performance of training from scratch on 100x more data' (semi-supervised setting on IMDb and AG).

claims.text: The BPTT technique for text classification is abbreviated as 'BPTB3C' in the summary.
claims.reason: The paper names this technique 'BPT3C' (BPTT for Text Classification), not 'BPTB3C' as written in the summary — an extra 'B' is inserted incorrectly.

claims.text: The paper is authored by 'Jeremy Howard et al.' implying a single primary author with additional contributors.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states 'Equal contribution' between Jeremy Howard and Sebastian Ruder, making them co-first authors, not a primary-with-others structure.
